title: 'Who Says There's No Theft in US?': Indian Family's Car Found Without Wheels
excerpt: The woman woke to find the family's parked car resting on supports with all four wheels gone — and a note left behind warning of a string of thefts at the parking lot.
body:
• An Indian family living in the US woke to find all four wheels of their parked car stolen overnight, with the vehicle left propped up on supports.
  • The thieves left behind a note warning residents about a string of thefts in the parking lot of a property identified as Crystal House, claiming at least three cars were vandalized in the past week.
  • A video of the wheel-less car has gone viral on social media, with the woman's Hindi remark — roughly, "who says there's no theft in the US?" — striking a chord with viewers in India.
  • The exact location and details have not been officially confirmed by police; the incident is being treated as unverified by authorities.

The Incident

An Indian family living in the United States woke up to an astonishing sight in their apartment parking lot: their car, stripped of all four wheels overnight, resting on supports the thieves had placed underneath to keep it from collapsing onto the ground.

https://x.com/Nation_First_X/status/2097659385988485365

In a video that has since gone viral on social media, the woman describes the shock of the discovery. When her brother woke up in the morning, she says, he found the car's wheels completely gone — the thieves had even propped the vehicle up on supports so it would not collapse after the wheels were removed.

"Kaun kehta hai US mein chori nahi hoti."

— The woman, in a viral video, as reported by Hindustan Times

The remark — "who says there is no theft in the US?" — has become the defining line of the episode, resonating with millions of viewers in India who associate the US with order and safety.

Context & Background

According to a note left behind at the scene, the theft was not an isolated incident. The note, posted in the parking lot of a property identified as Crystal House, warned residents that at least three cars had been vandalized in the past week and that wheels had been stolen from several vehicles. It raised questions about the management's responsibility for parking-lot safety and urged residents to raise their voice on the issue.

Wheel theft is a persistent problem in the US. Thieves target alloy wheels — which can fetch hundreds of dollars each on the resale market — and can strip a car in minutes with a jack and a lug wrench, often in the dead of night. Apartment complex parking lots, with limited surveillance and many parked cars, are among the most common hunting grounds.

The exact location of the incident and the full details of the theft have not been publicly revealed, and it has not been officially confirmed by the police, according to reports. The account rests on the viral video and the note left at the scene.

Impact & Analysis

Beyond the viral humor of the woman's remark lies a real financial blow. Replacing four wheels and tires can cost anywhere from $800 to several thousand dollars depending on the vehicle, and insurance deductibles often mean the owner pays a significant share out of pocket. For immigrant families budgeting carefully, that is a painful hit.

The incident also punctures a comforting myth. Many Indians arriving in the US carry an image of American suburbs and apartment complexes as essentially crime-free — an assumption the viral video has dismantled in a single frame of a car sitting on bricks. The note's claim of multiple thefts in one parking lot points to organized, repeat offending rather than a one-off crime of opportunity, and to the limited deterrence that parking-lot lighting and occasional patrols provide.

Security experts recommend simple precautions: parking in well-lit areas, using wheel locks (lug nut locks) that require a special key, and checking whether a renter's or auto insurance policy covers wheel theft specifically.

Diaspora Angle

The story has traveled fast in diaspora circles precisely because it is so relatable: a large share of Indian families in the US live in apartment complexes with shared, open parking lots, and car ownership is a necessity rather than a luxury. The woman's Hindi punchline captures a sentiment many immigrants recognize — the realization that the problems of back home, from petty theft to indifferent building management, exist on American soil too. It is a small, human story, but it speaks to the everyday texture of NRI life that rarely makes headlines.

What's Next

With the video circulating widely, pressure is likely to build on the property management at Crystal House to improve parking-lot security — better lighting, cameras, and controlled access. Whether the thieves are caught remains to be seen; wheel-theft cases are notoriously hard to solve without surveillance footage. For the family, the immediate task is the expensive business of getting their car back on four wheels — and, perhaps, investing in a set of wheel locks.
nri_angle: Many Indian families live in US apartment complexes with shared parking lots, and the incident has resonated widely with the diaspora — a familiar reminder that crime is a fact of life everywhere, not just back home.
author: Diaspora Desk
